title: Anthropic Revenue Jumps 14-Fold; Indian IT Faces AI Test
excerpt: Claude maker's $16.3 billion first half and IPO filing lifted chip stocks but knocked TCS and Infosys, even as AI passes 10% of their revenue
body:
• Anthropic, maker of the Claude models, reported first-half 2026 revenue of $16.3 billion, up 14-fold year on year, in disclosures tied to its US IPO filing under the ticker ANT on Nasdaq.
  • Indian IT shares fell up to 3% on Tuesday as the filing revived the AI-infrastructure trade: Infosys dropped 2.31% to Rs 1,139.05 and TCS fell 2.09% to Rs 2,481.90.
  • AI is already material for the Indian majors: TCS annualised AI revenue is $3.1 billion, Infosys AI revenue was 10.5% of its total and up 29% quarter on quarter, and HCLTech reported $219 million in advanced AI revenue, up 28.4% sequentially.
  • For investors, the test is arithmetic, not narrative: AI revenue must grow faster than AI-driven deflation shrinks traditional work — Infosys has already cut FY27 revenue growth guidance to 1%-2%.

Anthropic's move towards a US listing has put hard numbers on the artificial intelligence boom — and, for Indian IT investors, revived the question of whether that boom is a tailwind or a headwind. The Claude developer reported revenue of $16.3 billion for the six months ended June 30, 2026, a 14-fold increase from the same period a year earlier, according to disclosures reported from its IPO filing. The company formally registered with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on October 26, plans to list Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT, and had first submitted a draft registration confidentially on June 1, 2026. The number of shares and the price range have not been set.

Growth at a steep cost

The filing shows enterprise demand scaling quickly. Customers generating $100,000 or more in revenue over the past 12 months rose from more than 950 a year ago to more than 11,900 as of September 30, with over 1,900 customers above $1 million and nearly 250 above $10 million. Revenue from a subset of existing customers was more than nine times higher in the quarter ended September 30 than a year earlier. The costs are equally large. Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half, widened from $13 billion by accounting adjustments linked to the rising value of financial instruments, and computing and infrastructure costs of $8.95 billion in the first half alone. Cash, equivalents and short-term investments stood at $131.7 billion as of June 30.

Why Indian IT sold off

The market verdict was negative for services, positive for infrastructure. All 10 stocks in the NSE IT index traded lower, with the sector down roughly 1.5% in one update and individual names off up to 3%. Chip stocks moved the other way: the iShares Semiconductor ETF rose nearly 3%, Nvidia gained 2.4%, Micron rose 3%, Broadcom advanced 2.3% and AMD gained 2.8%, while Samsung and SK Hynix climbed about 4% or more. The logic, as analyst commentary summarised it, is that client budgets are still concentrated on AI infrastructure and computing capacity, while traditional maintenance and support work faces pricing pressure as clients demand AI productivity savings. Axis Mutual Fund remains underweight IT services on exactly that basis.

The bull case, in the companies' own numbers

The counter-argument is in the results. In the July-September quarter, AI crossed 10% of revenue at both TCS and Infosys for the first time. TCS reported annualised AI revenue of $3.1 billion, growing more than 19% over the quarter, alongside total second-quarter revenue of $7,642 million, up 2.4% year on year in dollar terms. Infosys reported AI at 10.5% of revenue, up 29% quarter on quarter, on second-quarter revenue of $5,145 million, and booked $5.2 billion in large-deal total contract value, including a mega deal above $2 billion. HCLTech reported advanced AI revenue of $219 million for the quarter, up 28.4% sequentially — about $876 million annualised — and raised the lower end of its FY27 constant-currency growth guidance to 2.5%-4%.

What analysts are watching

Brokerages are split on timing, not direction. Jefferies said the October rally — about Rs 3.87 lakh crore of market value recovered — was driven mainly by multiple expansion rather than earnings upgrades, leaving valuations sensitive to AI headlines. HSBC expects FY27 to be the sector's hardest year, with earnings growth slowing to 2%-3% before a mid-single-digit recovery. TCS chief executive K Krithivasan has acknowledged a deflationary effect from AI productivity gains while arguing that AI-led modernisation also creates vendor-consolidation opportunities. Analysts also caution that each company's AI revenue figure is self-defined and not directly comparable. For now, Anthropic's numbers prove demand for AI is real and enormous; whether TCS, Infosys and HCLTech convert that demand into faster overall growth — rather than simply replacing discounted legacy work — is the question the next two quarters of results will answer.
